Okay I feel as though I need to first give a short description of my background, I have a AS in computer network systems and a 3 weeks away from my BS in ISS (Information System Security) which is "Cyber Security", Network+/Security+. With regards to the actual game , I am impressed. I am often asked "How do I become a hacker?" at class and in this day in age , EVERYthing is monitored and recorded from phones to the sites you browse - truth be told you don't even know it because they tap you at the source (ISP or phone towers with devices such as Stingray for cell calls) without your knowledge. So its not really "teachable" without breaking a law of some sort - unless you setup your own private network with switches and servers (many people find this a daunting task in of itself) so I cannot help people in that regard. Anyway this "game" is very fun and if your familiar with basic Linux commands you will find that it is of great use to you, ive only played it for 20 minutes but working from mainly the command line I am very impressed. Its part fun and part real life - it almost feels like work, which is a good thing.

Holy crap. This game immersed me in a way no other game has for a long time. I won't go into the detail of the autheniticity of the simulator or the visuals or sound, as myriads before me have covered that. This game surprised me. Spoiler alert for those who wish to keep reading.

I saw the counter attack by the rogue hacker coming, and I thought there would be a way to prevent it. When the game BSODed, I thought "Oh! I guess it'll reset me just before the attack." But no, the game rattled to life again and forced me to think about how to restore my own pc, and that is something to be applauded in a game.
Then later I tried my hand at the CCC file dump, and lo and behold, I get traced, and suddenly the game gives me about 60 seconds to figure out how to hack my ISP and change my IP, while the trace is represented by your screen turning red. I was stressed and terriefied, and it was so, intense! Seriously, go try it for yourself. :)

I've just finished Hacknet, and as you can tell by my total playtime (which also includes a profile I didn't quite complete), it's not a very long game. However, I'm quite sure that you will love every minute of it.

I'm not entirely sure how this game stacks up if you just want another Uplink (I haven't played that particular game), but there are other reviews that focus on that. What I can tell you is that this game is a stylish, sleek, and very impressive hacking simulator. The plot is woven very well into the game, and there are easter eggs and hidden things aplenty. I made it a point to look at every IRC archive on every computer I hacked, because I'd be laughing even while they traced my IP address.

The game's solution to everything is elegant and new; nothing feels like a tired concept. The game is just long enough to be as impressive as possible with all of its assets.

On the negative side, the slightly buggy nature of the game is where the indie nature really shows. My first playthrough went well enough until I was hit with a progression-ending bug that I didn't realize until I had actually made progress into a hidden sidequest. From then on, I was a little bit afraid to explore and screw around in case I got hit with another glitch. An option to load from saves wouldn't be amiss, but I'm sure people would use it to save-scum (and unfortunately miss one of Hacknet's coolest features: [spoiler]attempting to forcibly reset your IP address just after a trace has reached your computer[/spoiler], which adds to the game's tension).

Some objectives and game aspects are a little unclear, especially when worded in the game's cool cyber-security lingo (which actually adds to the charm to some extent). For instance, there's only a small sliver of documentation about a considerably-important yet optional feature: setting up proxies as "traps" to be sprung if a trace is about to reach you, which overloads your computer but stops the trace from doing any lasting damage. Experimenting is rendered difficult due to the fear of bugs as above - again, some sort of feature to load a session might help.

However, above all, you will find that Hacknet is well worth your time and $10 (or $8 if you buy during this Steam sale), because - be honest with yourself - you're looking into Hacknet to feel like a Hollywood Hacker, and that's exactly what this game makes you feel like.

I have had much, MUCH more fun playing this than I expected.

A combination of a clever plot, interesting puzzles, atmospheric music and a well managed difficulty curve makes it very easy to lose yourself entirely to being the hacker that we all saw in films in the early 2000's.  Only actualy capable of using a computer.

The game starts you off with a straight-forward set of tools, which rapidly expands to meet the various challenges you meet.  By the end, I was utterly enthralled by and immersed in the game.

It's more story based than the obvious comparison, Uplink, so you do less in the way of freelance hacking.  It would have been nice to have the option to be slightly more mercenary, but the story blossoms as you approach the climax of the game - motivating you emotionaly as well as intellectualy to see the game through.

What's more, there are lots of little easter eggs you can find, people's activities you can track and secret activies to uncover - if you know your way around the computer languages the game is built around I have no doubt that there are even more possibilities.  I haven't, but I didn't feel that I was missing anything.

I would seriously reccomend givng this game a go, its been a while since I've played a game that made me feel genuinely clever - neither led-by-the-hand nor over-faced by its challenges.

[H1]So I heard you like command line interfaces...[/H1]

Hacknet takes cues from a mix of places, primarily Hacker Evolution and Uplink, creating a blend that can safely be summed up as a hacking puzzle sim. Your job is to utilise the tools you acquire to probe and gain access to a selection of progressively trickier systems and networks, and unravel the story of a hacker who recently deceased in a supposed accident. Initially you're given control of HackNet, a revolutionary OS that makes you essentially invincible from traditional tracing methods, and a few basic tools, from there your job is to gather the resources you'll need to piece together the mystery of what happened.

[H1]A lot closer to the real thing than I expected...[/H1]

Hacknet hews a lot closer to the real nature of exploiting individual ports (even if the programs are automated and require little work to figure out the relevant exploits), and you'll be picking apart servers step by step, usually using command line textual input which makes the game "feel" an awful lot more real than say, Uplink (though uplink succeeded much more from a neuromancer perspective). You'll be learning the concept of using shells to overwhelm proxies, cyclical analysis and syndication to deal with firewalls, and the use of various tools to pry open specific ports to eventually use your swiss army knife tool "PortHack" which will then turn over Admin control of a system to you. Then you get to explore, and use various commands to remove evidence of your tomfoolery.

[H1]Oh Bash, you wonderful meme generator...[/H1]

The game is LOADED with internet culture references, the devs made liberal use of bash.org for IRC logs which litter the servers, taking a "best of" the IRC culture and invariably having some real funnies tucked away on the servers for you to discover, along with various text files with references to games and other internet geekery. There's a lot that's relevant and interesting, and you'll no doubt enjoy what you find as you explore the various servers. There's also hidden paths, servers lying out of the way, and secret side dishes for those willing to investigate and probe various elements of the games rather cavernous depths.

[H1]A stylish presentation[/H1]

The game is presented in a very slick x-term package, anyone who's used X11 interfaces in Linux will be very much at home here, and more entertainingly, there's the ability to replace your xterm with ones you find, changing up your wallpaper and colour scheme as you progress through the game. The music too, is very well thought out, and very appropriate, with music that's contextual to various events kicking in and ensuring that you get pumped up at just the right times. Even the HackNet OS boot sequence is pleasingly authentic, right down to little details such as memory allocations and devices and the like.

[H1]Closing thoughts[/H1]

The one big criticism is that this game is hand crafted, this is both a strength AND a weakness, because unlike Uplink, once you've finished the game and plumbed out all the secrets, there isn't much more to come back to. However, what there IS that's here, and there's a good 6-8 hours, is stylish, well written, and very nicely presented. Not to mention a great callback to -good- hacking games, which is something that's been sorely missing as of late.

[b]Verdict : Highly recommended[/b]

Right, where do I begin?

Hacknet is a game with a lot of potential. I enjoyed it thoroughly, found the story to be very engaging, and the "think fast" moments were executed well enough for some noticeable pressure to kick in. The music and visuals work *really* well together to deliver a captivating experience.

However, Hacknet is not quite at a stage where I'd call it a full release. Right now, it looks more like a competent early access preview. The game is riddled with game-breaking bugs (What's that? You're a completionist and decided to do all quests for one faction before moving on to the next? I'm afraid you just got the storyline out of sync and will find yourself stuck shortly!) and a bit too short to make a strong case for the price tag. The severity of the bugs is somewhat mitigated by the simplicity of the save file format, so if you end up screwing yourself over, you can cheat your way around it.

All in all, Hacknet is a less advanced but still oh-so-enjoyable Uplink. If you already know Uplink and are looking for more of the same, you'll enjoy Hacknet despite its flaws. Since the game is still being actively patched by the dev, it will hopefully become even better over time.

So,  wait no more :) Play it! Get hooked!

reviews.review:
Really impressed! Having played Uplink and the like, I've fallen in love with this game which is much more realistic and somehow less cumbersome at the same time. A lot of old cliches are simplified down, you get a 99sec timer instead of repetitively bouncing connections around a map. You can remove all log files with a single command instead of running through each one with a log deleter and worrying about leaving suspicious deletions.

So what replaces all this? The game puts much more emphasis on discovery and exploration, chasing through IRC logs and network maps to find other computers to break into. Missions are scripted, story-based, and much more interesting than Uplink's procedural "delete this, copy that, forge this" procedural mission list.

There's still breaking past firewalls and proxies, and it's handled the same way as Uplink. UNIX shell knowledge is advised although this would be a great introduction for someone wanting to learn. The command list isn't too big or complex, but it doesn't try to cater to the average bloke-on-the-street either as shown by it's five-minute barebones tutorial.

Maybe it's not bringing a whole lot of new gameplay to the table as some have described, but what it does it seems to do very well. Also have not come across any bugs yet. Great game that seems clearly inspired by the now classic PC game, Uplink. Like Uplink, it takes the idea of hacking and simplifies it, but Hacknet attempts to keep it more grounded. While still pretty far from reality, if you have worked in a terminal before you'll be right at home immediately. I might be wrong, but I'm pretty sure you could complete almost the entire game from just the terminal without ever using the GUI elements. That said, there is a GUI for almost everything and it is a very simple game to get into even if you don't know very much about computers. It simplifies everything in a way that makes it easy enough for anyone to pickup, but still satisfying when you complete your tasks. The game is a bit on the easy side, but there are some cool secrets to find that are a bit more complicated.

I'm not sure what the developer has planned in the future, but I'll definitely be keeping an eye on their future games!

This game is about hacking as the name implies, starting you off with a bare few programs and growing your arsenal as you progress its storyline. This game stands as a spiritual successor to Uplink bar a few features that keep it from reaching Uplink's cult following, but still make the game interesting and make me wish the two games had merged into one supergame with the visuals of Hacknet and the in-depth sandbox nature of Uplink.

Starting with a bootup sequence, an automated message box by the "Bit" character and a tutorial program with a cool digital background soundtrack sets the tone for the game immediately. Given basic instructions to hack your first terminal can take time to figure out even with the tutorials. Learning these commands will be the bread and butter of this game, and so with every successful command you'll be rewarded with a visual representation of the program functioning to unlock ports or simply find a password.

This game doesn't rely on money for upgrades, and in turn missions do not give money but instead increases your rank. Increasing your rank will allow you bigger missions, and will grant you access to servers to download more powerful programs which will allow you to crack more secure servers and reveal that the missions lead a linear path with admittedly little room to shift the way the story goes.

Like Uplink, this can be a very short and very easy game to get through if you know what you're doing. This is made easier with the ability to save and the Trace Aversion game, should you lag behind or stay on a server while being traced and run out of time. The Trace Aversion sequence isn't anything special in terms of gameplay, but you will be given a timelimit to hack a server and type in your IP address to avert a game over, requiring a few midgame tools at the least.

I've yet to finish the game, and I've recently gotten stuck at a point where I require a program from another mission before I can finish my current mission. I'd advise doing everything you can before starting the endgame, because there's some programs hidden behind locked missions waiting for you to reach the top rank before allowing you to take them, these missions hold programs that are required for the end game. There's also a few guides available for the little confusing things, in which they are in abundance.

Overall I do like what I've seen, and there's definitely a charming nature that comes from these hacking games with Hacknet being no different. I'd recommend it for anyone interested in simulations, puzzles, and anyone who just likes to solve things on their own. This is Hollywood hacking at its core though, and it doesn't represent real techniques used by actual hackers.

Unfortunately the story also has a few bugs at the moment (e.g. the juneberg mission never got activated for me and so i was unable to get one tool needed to continue without a workaround).
I think it's a bit problematic that you can only accept one contract at a time and some missions are activated automatically.

I'm a huge fan of uplink and so i enjoyed this game as well but uplink has much more depth to it.
In hacknet the hacking tools all work the same and you just need to run them.
In uplink you got crackers (pasword, decypher), voice analyzer, bypasses, LANs, ... everything in different versions and you can also upgrade your hardware.

On the plus side there's not so much grinding in this game compared to uplink. No server bouncing and single log file clearing on different machines.
Furthermore i really, really enjoyed using the console. Almost everything is console based and there is syntax completion!

So all in all i would recommend this game to die-hard uplink fans looking for something similar.

The best "hacking" simulator I've ever played. I've been playing almost nonstop since I purchased the game and for a game to hold my attention for this many hours is surprising. Highly recommended, GREAT GAME!
